{{DISPLAYTITLE:Syntax extension and hygienic macros}}
{{Plebeian|Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Programs and proofs in one language}}
{{Lean theorem prover map}}

Lean's grammar is not fixed. A Lean source file can add operators, notations and whole new
syntactic forms, and say what each one means by rewriting it into syntax Lean already
understands. The rewriting is done by '''macros''', and Lean's macros are '''hygienic''': a
name that a macro introduces cannot capture a name the user wrote, and a name the user wrote
cannot capture one the macro relies on. This page shows the commands, from the simplest
(<code>infixl</code>) to the most general (<code>macro_rules</code>), and what hygiene
prevents, with examples compiled by Lean 4.34.1. The design is set out by Ullrich and de
Moura.<ref name="bn">Sebastian Ullrich and Leonardo de Moura, "Beyond Notations: Hygienic Macro Expansion for Theorem Proving Languages", ''Logical Methods in Computer Science'' 18(2), 2022, article 1, 21 pp. Extended version of the paper in ''Automated Reasoning: IJCAR 2020'', Lecture Notes in Computer Science 12167, Springer, 2020, pp. 167–182 (doi:10.1007/978-3-030-51054-1_10). doi:[https://doi.org/10.46298/lmcs-18(2:1)2022 10.46298/lmcs-18(2:1)2022]; preprint [https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.10490 arXiv:2001.10490].</ref>

== Where syntax extension sits ==

Lean reads a source file one command at a time. Each command is parsed, then
[[Lean theorem prover/System/Elaboration|elaborated]] into terms of the type theory, and only
the elaborated result is passed to the Lean kernel. Macro expansion happens after parsing, as
part of elaboration: before a piece of syntax is elaborated, any macro at its outermost layer
is expanded.<ref name="rm-macros" /> A macro takes a piece of syntax and returns another piece of syntax; the
reference manual calls the expansion of a notation "a purely syntactic process that occurs
prior to elaboration or code generation".<ref name="rm-notations">"Notations", section 23.3 of ''The Lean Language Reference'' (edition covering Lean 4.34.0). [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Notations-and-Macros/Notations/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Notations-and-Macros/Notations/]</ref>
Whatever a macro produces is then elaborated and checked exactly as if the user had typed
it. A macro can change what is written; it cannot prove anything that the text it produces
could not prove if typed by hand.

The commands form a tower. The operator commands are shorthands for <code>notation</code>.
In Ullrich and de Moura's account, <code>notation</code> is itself a macro that generates a
<code>macro</code>, and <code>macro</code> expands into a grammar rule (<code>syntax</code>)
paired with a rewriting rule (<code>macro_rules</code>).<ref name="bn" /><ref name="rm-ops" />
In Lean 4.34.1, <code>notation</code> and <code>macro</code> are each handled by an
elaborator that produces this pair directly.<ref name="src-notation">Lean 4 source code, version 4.34.1 (2026), files <code>src/Lean/Elab/Notation.lean</code> (the functions <code>elabNotation</code> and <code>mkUnexpander</code>) and <code>src/Lean/Elab/Macro.lean</code> (the function <code>elabMacro</code>). Apache License 2.0. https://github.com/leanprover/lean4/blob/v4.34.1/src/Lean/Elab/Notation.lean</ref> The
<code>syntax</code> and <code>macro_rules</code> commands in turn become ordinary Lean
definitions that the parser and the macro expander consult.<ref name="bn" />

== Operators ==

The smallest extension names a binary operator.

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
def avg (a b : Nat) : Nat := (a + b) / 2

infixl:65 " ⊞ " => avg

#eval 2 ⊞ 4 ⊞ 10
#check fun (a b : Nat) => avg a b
</pre>

The <code>#eval</code> prints <code>6</code>: the operator associates to the left, so the
expression is <code>avg (avg 2 4) 10</code>, that is <code>avg 3 10</code>. The reference
manual gives the expansion exactly: <code>infixl:prec "op" => f</code> stands for
<code>notation:prec x:prec "op" y:prec1 => f x y</code>, where <code>prec1</code> is one more
than <code>prec</code>, so the left operand may itself be a use of the operator and the right
operand may not. A custom operator must state its precedence; there is no default.<ref name="rm-ops">"Custom Operators", section 23.1 of ''The Lean Language Reference'' (edition covering Lean 4.34.0). [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Notations-and-Macros/Custom-Operators/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Notations-and-Macros/Custom-Operators/]</ref>

The <code>#check</code> shows the other direction. Asked to print <code>avg a b</code>, Lean
prints

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">fun a b => a ⊞ b : Nat → Nat → Nat</pre>

The command has also generated an '''unexpander''', a rule used when terms are displayed. A
notation gets one when its right-hand side applies a named function and each of its term
positions occurs there exactly once; a notation that expands to an anonymous function gets
none.<ref name="rm-notations" /><ref name="rm-ops" />
The operator therefore appears in goals and error messages, not only in source text.

== Notation, syntax and macro rules ==

<code>notation</code> accepts any mixture of tokens and term positions, and its right-hand
side is a template. When a template is not enough, the two halves can be written separately.
<code>syntax</code> adds a grammar rule to a '''syntax category''' (here <code>term</code>),
and <code>macro_rules</code> says how to rewrite it.

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
syntax "∑ " ident " ∈ " term ", " term : term

macro_rules
  | `(∑ $i ∈ $xs, $body) => `(List.foldl (fun acc $i => acc + $body) 0 $xs)

#eval ∑ i ∈ [1, 2, 3, 4], i * i
</pre>

The output is <code>30</code>, the sum of the squares of 1 to 4. The pattern on the left of
<code>=></code> and the result on the right are '''syntax quotations''', written
<code>`(...)</code>. Inside them <code>$i</code>, <code>$xs</code> and <code>$body</code> are
'''antiquotations''': holes that match syntax in a pattern and insert it in a result. A
quotation produces syntax, not a term; it is parsed but not elaborated.<ref name="rm-macros">"Macros", section 23.5 of ''The Lean Language Reference'' (edition covering Lean 4.34.0), including 23.5.1 "Hygiene", 23.5.3 "Quotation" and 23.5.5 "Defining Macros". [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Notations-and-Macros/Macros/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Notations-and-Macros/Macros/]</ref>

<code>macro_rules</code> is open. More rules for the same syntax may be added later, in the
same file or another, and the most recently defined is tried first. A rule that does not
apply hands the syntax on to the next one, by throwing the exception
<code>unsupportedSyntax</code>; any other exception is reported as an error. Only the
outermost layer of syntax is expanded at a time, and nested macros are expanded when the
elaborator reaches them.<ref name="rm-macros" />

Syntax categories are not limited to terms. Commands and tactics are categories too, and a
library may declare its own with <code>declare_syntax_cat</code>. Ullrich and de Moura give an
example of why this matters: a big-operator file in Coq's Mathematical Components library
repeats twelve notations for index ranges once for each of three operators, because Coq's
notation system cannot abstract over the index syntax; with a category for index ranges,
each range form is interpreted once and every operator reuses it.<ref name="bn" />

== What hygiene prevents ==

A macro is a function on syntax, and syntax contains names. Two kinds of accident follow
from that.

The first is '''variable capture''': a binder the macro introduces captures a name the user
supplied. Ullrich and de Moura's example is a notation for constant
functions.<ref name="bn" />

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
notation "const" e => fun x => e

#check fun (x : Nat) => const x
#eval (fun (x : Nat) => const x) 1 2
</pre>

Read as text substitution, <code>const x</code> becomes <code>fun x => x</code>, the
identity, and the whole expression would return its second argument. Lean prints

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">fun x x_1 => x : (x : Nat) → ?m.2 x → Nat
1</pre>

The binder that the notation introduced has been renamed (Lean displays it as
<code>x_1</code>), the user's <code>x</code> still refers to the outer binder, and the
function returns its first argument. The mechanism is the '''macro scope'''. Each expansion of
a macro tags every identifier it introduces with a fresh scope, and a binder and a use of a
name match only if their tags agree.<ref name="rm-macros" /><ref name="bn" /> The user's
<code>x</code> carries no tag and the macro's carries one, so they are different names.

Hygiene can be switched off, and the same notation then captures.

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
set_option hygiene false in
notation "const'" e => fun x => e

#eval (fun (x : Nat) => const' x) 1 2
</pre>

This prints <code>2</code>, and Lean's linter warns that the outer <code>x</code> is never
referenced: the macro's binder has taken it. The summation notation above is protected in
the same way. Its accumulator is called <code>acc</code>, and a user's variable of that name
is not affected.

<pre class="lean lean-cont" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
#eval let acc := 100; ∑ i ∈ [1, 2, 3], acc * i
</pre>

The result is <code>600</code>. Rewritten by plain substitution, the body
<code>acc * i</code> would refer to the accumulator, which starts at 0, and the result would
be 0.

The second kind of accident runs the other way: a local name at the use site captures a
global name the macro relies on.

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
def double (n : Nat) : Nat := 2 * n

macro "dbl! " e:term : term => `(double $e)

#eval let double := fun (n : Nat) => n; dbl! 5
</pre>

The output is <code>10</code>, and Lean warns that the local variable <code>double</code> is
not referenced. The identifier <code>double</code> in the quotation carries the macro's scope
and the local binding at the use site does not, so the two do not match. When the quotation
<code>`(double $e)</code> was compiled, the name was also resolved to the global function and
recorded with it, so a global of the same name introduced later cannot redirect it
either.<ref name="rm-macros" /><ref name="bn" />

== Hygiene in tactics ==

Tactics form a syntax category, so a tactic can be a macro (the
[[Lean theorem prover/System/The tactic framework|tactic framework]] treats the result like
any other tactic). This one introduces a hypothesis and uses it.

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
macro "intro_assumption" : tactic => `(tactic| (intro h; exact h))

example (p : Prop) : p → p := by intro_assumption
</pre>

The proof is accepted. The name <code>h</code>, however, belongs to the macro. A script that
uses a macro to introduce <code>h</code> and then refers to <code>h</code> itself fails.

<pre class="lean lean-fails" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
macro "intro_hyp" : tactic => `(tactic| intro h)

example (p : Prop) : p → p := by
  intro_hyp
  exact h
</pre>

Lean reports <code>Unknown identifier `h`</code> at the last line. The hypothesis exists,
but under a name the user cannot type:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
macro "intro_hyp" : tactic => `(tactic| intro h)

example (p : Prop) : p → p := by
  intro_hyp
  trace_state
  assumption
</pre>

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">p : Prop
h✝ : p
⊢ p</pre>

The dagger marks an inaccessible name, and <code>assumption</code>, which does not need the
name, closes the goal. Ullrich and de Moura report that Lean 3's tactic quotations had both
faults: a short tactic script for injectivity lemmas broke when it was used from a library
for homotopy type theory that defined its own <code>propext</code> and
<code>Iff.intro</code>, and scripts could refer to names a tactic had introduced. They
describe Lean 4's tactic language as, to their knowledge, the first in an established theorem
prover to be hygienic automatically in this sense.<ref name="bn" />

== Mathematics in its own notation ==

Mathematics is written in notation that varies by field and by author, and much of it binds
variables: sums, products, integrals, set-builder notation, quantifiers over a finite set. A
fixed grammar forces a formal text away from that notation. Lean's macros let a library add
it, with three properties that matter in practice.

Binding notation is safe to define. A notation that introduces its own bound variables, such
as the sum above, does not interfere with the names its user chooses, and the user need not
know which names it uses inside. Without hygiene, every such notation would be a hazard of
the kind shown in the <code>const</code> example.

Notation is printed back. Because an unexpander is generated where possible, goals and error
messages show the notation the reader wrote, not the function it stands for.

Notation can be confined. A notation marked <code>scoped</code> is active only where its
namespace is open, so a field's notation need not occupy the grammar of every other field.

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
def avg (a b : Nat) : Nat := (a + b) / 2

namespace Averages
scoped infixl:65 " ⊞ " => avg
end Averages

open Averages in
#eval 2 ⊞ 4 ⊞ 10
</pre>

This prints <code>6</code>. Without the <code>open</code>, <code>⊞</code> is not part of the
grammar:

<pre class="lean lean-fails" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
def avg (a b : Nat) : Nat := (a + b) / 2

namespace Averages
scoped infixl:65 " ⊞ " => avg
end Averages

#check (2 ⊞ 4 : Nat)
</pre>

Lean stops at the operator with the parse error <code>expected token</code>.

What notation does not do is add meaning. It changes how a statement is written and read,
and nothing that the Lean kernel checks. That is also its risk. A statement that uses
unfamiliar notation may not say what it appears to say, and the reference manual's guidance
on validating a proof names custom notation among the things to investigate when there is
doubt that a theorem states what was intended.<ref name="rm-validating">"Validating a Lean Proof", a chapter of ''The Lean Language Reference'' (edition covering Lean 4.34.0), section "Remaining Issues". [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/ValidatingProofs/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/ValidatingProofs/]</ref>

A macro sees only syntax. When a translation depends on types, for example on whether an
argument is a natural number or a set, a macro cannot decide it, and an '''elaborator''' is
needed: a Lean program that runs inside the elaborator and constructs terms directly.
